To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
intrathoracic LES function is impaired by the absence of vagal tone and that restoration of competence is associated with elongation of the LES.

intrathoracic LES displacement results in decreased resting pressure and in decreased response to compression, that vagotomy results in decreased resting LES pressure and decreased response to compression and that fundic wrap and abdominal LES replacement results in increased resting LES pressure, elongation of the LES and increased response to compression.

the function of the LES is influenced by the intrathoracic position of the LES, and that fundic-wrap combined with replacement of the LES below the level of the diaphragm is more effective in restoring gastroesophageal competency than replacement of the LES alone.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

intrathoracic position of the LES, per se, is not the only factor responsible for the failure of the LES to respond to abdominal compression, and that restoration of competence is not simply a function of the LES being placed in the abdomen.

the LES is not a sphincter in the strict anatomic sense, but a functional unit which is dependent on both the intrathoracic position of the LES and the integrity of the extrinsic innervation of the LES.
the LES is not a sphincter in the true sense of the word, but is a zone of high pressure that is maintained by tonic vagal input.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the LES can be restored to normal function by replacing it below the diaphragms, and that the most effective way to do this is to combine fundic wrap with abdominal LES replacement.
the LES is a dynamic structure which is influenced by its environment.
the function of the LES is influenced by the position of the LES within the abdomen, and that the function of a vagotomized, intrathoracic LES is restored by replacing it below the diaphragms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the function of the LES is influenced by its intrathoracic position.
the LES is not a sphincter per se but rather an elongated high pressure zone.
